youtube.title: Strait of Hormuz: The 33 km Gap a Fifth of the World's Oil Must Cross
youtube.description:
Every day about 20 million barrels of oil, roughly a fifth of what the world uses, sail through one narrow gap between Iran and Oman. Why has no one found a way round it, and who decides whether it stays open?

On the map: the two-mile shipping lanes, the islands still disputed between Iran and the UAE, five centuries of empires that held the gate, the two readings of the law of the sea, the pipelines built to avoid it, and three ways the map could change. Every figure is sourced, and where sources disagree we say so.

{CHAPTERS}

sources.claim: About 20 million barrels a day pass through the Strait of Hormuz
sources.source: US Energy Information Administration (EIA), 'Amid regional conflict, the Strait of Hormuz remains critical oil chokepoint', 16 June 2025 (2024 average)

sources.claim: That is about a fifth of the world's petroleum liquids consumption
The EIA gives the narrowest width as 21 miles, about 33 km
sources.source: EIA, World Oil Transit Chokepoints, and EIA, 16 June 2025

sources.claim: Britannica gives the strait's width as 55 to 95 km
Each shipping lane is two miles wide, with a two-mile buffer between them
Tension near the strait has moved crude prices before: Brent rose by as much as 4% after two tankers were attacked in the Gulf of Oman
69% of Hormuz crude and condensate flows in 2024 went to China, India, Japan and South Korea
84% of the crude and condensate through Hormuz in 2024 went to Asian markets
About a fifth of global LNG trade passes through Hormuz, mostly from Qatar
Saudi Arabia moves more crude through Hormuz than any other country
The Gulf is about 990 km long and rarely deeper than 90 m
Musandam is an exclave of Oman separated from the rest of Oman by UAE territory
Coastal states may claim a territorial sea of up to 12 nautical miles
sources.source: UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), Article 3, 10 December 1982

sources.claim: The shipping lanes through the narrows lie in Omani territorial waters
sources.source: Robert Strauss Center for International Security and Law, 'Strait of Hormuz' project (University of Texas at Austin)

sources.claim: Qatar's North Field and Iran's South Pars are one gas reservoir
Unused bypass pipeline capacity is about 2.6 million barrels a day
Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline runs about 1,200 km to Yanbu, capacity 5 million b/d
sources.source: EIA, 16 June 2025; EIA Saudi Arabia country analysis

sources.claim: In 2019 Saudi Arabia temporarily raised East-West capacity to 7 million b/d by converting gas-liquids lines
The UAE's Habshan-Fujairah pipeline can carry 1.5 million b/d
Hormuz was the seat of a trading kingdom in 1507 when Albuquerque's fleet arrived
Albuquerque returned in 1515 and took the island; the Portuguese fortress was built
Portugal issued passes, cartazes, to ships trading in waters it claimed
sources.source: Sanjay Subrahmanyam, The Portuguese Empire in Asia, 1500-1700 (1993)

sources.claim: In 1622 Shah Abbas I took Hormuz with English East India Company ships
Bandar Abbas is named after Shah Abbas
Britain signed treaties with the southern Gulf sheikhdoms in 1820 and 1853; they became known as the Trucial States
In January 1968 Britain announced withdrawal of its forces from the Gulf by the end of 1971
sources.source: UK House of Commons, Hansard, statement on public expenditure, 16 January 1968

sources.claim: Iranian forces landed on Abu Musa and the Greater and Lesser Tunb on 30 November 1971
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Abu Musa'; Richard Schofield (ed.), Territorial Foundations of the Gulf States (1994)

sources.claim: Abu Musa was covered by an Iran-Sharjah memorandum of November 1971; the Tunbs were claimed by Ras al-Khaimah
The UAE was formed on 2 December 1971 and claims all three islands
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'United Arab Emirates'; GCC Supreme Council communiqués (annual)

sources.claim: Iran says the islands are Iranian and not negotiable; the UAE calls them occupied and seeks talks or the ICJ
sources.source: Iranian Foreign Ministry statements; GCC Supreme Council final communiqués (e.g. December 2023)

sources.claim: From 1984 Iraq and Iran attacked each other's oil shipping, the Tanker War, to 1988
sources.source: US Naval Institute, 'The Tanker War', Proceedings, May 1988; Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Iran-Iraq War'

sources.claim: In 1987 the US reflagged and escorted Kuwaiti tankers
sources.source: US Naval History and Heritage Command, 'Operation Earnest Will'

sources.claim: On 18 April 1988 the US Navy struck Iranian platforms and ships after a mine hit the USS Samuel B. Roberts on 14 April
sources.source: US Naval History and Heritage Command, 'Operation Praying Mantis'

sources.claim: The US Fifth Fleet was re-formed in 1995, based in Bahrain
sources.source: US Naval Forces Central Command, 'Fifth Fleet history'

sources.claim: UNCLOS was signed on 10 December 1982; Article 38 creates transit passage, which shall not be impeded; Article 44: bordering states shall not hamper it
Iran signed UNCLOS in 1982 but has not ratified it; its declaration says transit passage rights apply only to states party
sources.source: UN Treaty Collection, UNCLOS status and declarations (Iran, 10 December 1982)

sources.claim: The US has not joined UNCLOS and holds that transit passage is customary international law
sources.source: US Department of State, Limits in the Seas / Maritime Claims Reference Manual

sources.claim: Oman ratified UNCLOS in 1989
sources.source: UN Treaty Collection, UNCLOS status (Oman, 17 August 1989)

sources.claim: Iran's navy and the IRGC navy have bases along the northern shore including Bandar Abbas
sources.source: Congressional Research Service, 'Iran's Foreign and Defense Policies' (updated 2024)

sources.claim: Rouhani proposed the Hormuz Peace Endeavour at the UN in 2019
sources.source: UN General Assembly, address by Iran's President, 25 September 2019

sources.claim: In December 2011 Iran's vice-president warned no oil would pass Hormuz if sanctions targeted its exports
On 4 July 2019 Gibraltar, with Royal Marines, detained the tanker Grace 1 on suspicion of carrying oil to Syria against EU sanctions
sources.source: Government of Gibraltar statement, 4 July 2019; BBC News, 4 July 2019

sources.claim: On 19 July 2019 the IRGC seized the British-flagged Stena Impero; Iran cited maritime violations; the UK called it illegal
sources.source: Reuters, 19-20 July 2019; UK Foreign Office statement, July 2019

sources.claim: Tankers were damaged off Fujairah on 12 May 2019 and in the Gulf of Oman on 13 June 2019; the US blamed Iran, which denied it
In April 2024 the IRGC seized the container ship MSC Aries near the strait
In June 2025 Iran's parliament backed closing the strait, with the final decision for the Supreme National Security Council; the strait stayed open
sources.source: Reuters, 22 June 2025; EIA, 16 June 2025 and later shipping data

sources.claim: Iran has never fully closed the strait, including during the Tanker War
sources.source: Congressional Research Service, 'Iran's Threats, the Strait of Hormuz, and Oil Markets' (R42335, 2012)

sources.claim: A US-led maritime security mission was formed in 2019, headquartered in Bahrain
sources.source: International Maritime Security Construct, launch statements, November 2019

sources.claim: Iran loaded its first cargo at Jask from the Goreh-Jask pipeline in July 2021
Oman hosted US-Iran talks in Muscat in April 2025
About 17.4 million b/d would have no pipeline route (20 minus 2.6)
IEA net-importing members must hold oil stocks of at least 90 days of net imports
sources.source: International Energy Agency, 'Oil stocks of IEA countries' (emergency response rules)

sources.claim: Iraq and Jordan agreed in 2013 on a Basra-Aqaba pipeline; it has not been built
sources.source: Reuters, 9 April 2013; later Reuters reporting through 2023

sources.claim: QatarEnergy plans to raise LNG capacity from 77 to 142 million tonnes a year before the end of the decade
The IEA projected oil demand peaking before 2030 under stated policies
OPEC projected demand rising to about 120 million b/d in 2050
Bab el-Mandeb is 18 miles wide at its narrowest
Since late 2023, attacks on shipping in the Red Sea sent many ships round Africa
sources.source: EIA, 'Red Sea chokepoints are critical for international oil and natural gas flows', 2024; UNCTAD, February 2024
